analytic.title: On the Complexity of Scheduling Real-Time Tasks with Self-Suspensions on One Processor

div.p: Integrating practical factors in scheduling theory is a major issue. Efficient schedulability tests (polynomial time or pseudo-polynomial time algorithms) are known for preemptive, independent tasks. In this paper, tasks are allowed to self-suspend. In practice, the real-time kernel suspends a task when it requests an external blocking operation. We study feasibility analysis problems from the computational complexity point of view. The problem is proved AEÈ-hard in the strong sense for periodic, preemptive or non-preemptive task sets. If we allow tasks to have several flows of control (multi-threaded tasks), then the corresponding feasibility problem is shown to be AEÈ-hard in the strong sense in the case of unit execution time threads.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In hard real-time systems, guaranteeing that tasks meet their deadlines is a major concern. Real-time processes are typically implemented as an event-driven code embedded within an infinite loop. A task is said to be schedulable (or feasible) if the scheduling policy implies that every deadline is met. Timing constraints are verified by performing an offline schedulability analysis. The first step in this analysis involves obtaining an equivalent task model for the code. The first model proposed in the literature characterizes a task by an execution requirement and a period between two successive releases of the task in the system [17]. Several models for hard real-time tasks have been proposed to deal with practical applications. Processes that are implemented as straight-line code (i.e. code with no conditional branches) within an infinite loop can often be transformed to sporadic tasks [18] or generalized multiframe tasks [3]. In order to deal with conditional real-time code, two models have been proposed: the recurring branching model [1] and the recur-ring real-time task model [2]. Discussions on other types of models can be found in [8] and [12].

Most schedulability tests assume that no task ever suspends itself. When a task invokes an external operation (I/O call or a remote procedure on a specialized processor), it always performs a system call of the kernel that suspends the job until the external operation becomes completed. The task is blocked and its descriptor is stored in the blocked queue of the invoked service. The scheduler chooses the next task to be executed among those stored in the ready queue. When the external operation is completed, the kernel moves the suspended task from the blocked queue to the ready queue. Sufficient schedulability tests are presented in [19,14] for fixed-priority tasks with self-suspension. These tests are both based on a time-demand analysis method, leading to sufficient schedulability conditions, computed in pseudo-polynomial time.

Schedulability analysis of a real-time system leads to a decision problem in the field of computational complexity theory: does a schedule exist, such that the completion times of the tasks are less than or equal to their deadlines? In practice, the computational complexity theory helps us to select adapted methods in order to solve the feasibility problem. When tasks are allowed to self-suspend, the feasibility problem becomes harder to solve. This is mainly due to suspension delays that introduce additional timing constraints.

The definition of the schedulability problem is very sensitive to the release times of the tasks. Changing the release time of a task in a schedulable real-time system can lead to a task missing its deadline. In practice, designers of real-time systems have varying degrees of control over the release times [4,11]. This leads to different feasibility problems. If release times can be chosen freely then the decision problem is the offset-free schedulability problem: do release times exist for which the tasks are schedulable? If nothing in particular is known about the starting times of the tasks then the schedulability problem will be stated as the nonconcrete schedulability problem: is the task system schedulable whatever the release times are? Lastly, if the release times are known, then it defines the concrete schedulability problem: is the task system schedulable for the given release times?

In the remainder of the paper, we consider the computational complexity of the uniprocessor concrete schedulability problem when tasks are allowed to self-suspend. We assume that release times and self-suspension delays of tasks are known. We assume the suspension delays to be nonnegative integers. The task model and known computational complexity results are presented in Section 2. Section 3 presents the complexity results for sequential tasks, both in preemptive and non-preemptive dispatching strategies. Section 4 proves the AEÈ-hardness of multi-threaded task sets.

div.head: The model and known computational complexity results
The multi-threaded task model
div.p: Multi-threaded tasks are implemented in most real-time operating systems. Such tasks are decomposed into a set of threads that can be concurrently executed by the processor. Thus, a task can be defined by several flows of control. We model a multi-threaded task by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where vertices are portions of the code and edges the suspension delays between them. In order to simplify the terminology, a thread is a portion of the code without self-suspension belonging to a task.

div.p: In Definition 1, self-suspension delays are defined as non-negative integers. This might not be the case in realistic applications. However, lower and upper bounds of suspension delays can be established by using best-case and worst-case analysis. Then, we limit ourselves to a particular case where upper bounds and lower bounds coincide with non-negative integers. This assumption will simplify AEÈ-hardness proofs.

Note that the task model proposed in Definition 1 is different from the recurring real-time task model presented in [2] (also based on a DAG modeling of tasks). In this latter model, releases of dependent jobs are separated by a minimum separation time. In our model, timing constraints are between completions of threads and starting times of their successors. Furthermore, all threads (corresponding to the vertices) are scheduled in our model; whereas jobs belonging to a path of each task graph will be scheduled for recurring real-time tasks.
We now define sequential tasks as a particular case of multi-threaded tasks.
Definition 2 A multi-threaded task is sequential if the associated DAG is a chain.

Input threads (respectively output threads) of a task , are those having no predecessor (respectively successor) in the DAG associated to . Without loss of generality if a task has several input threads, we assume that they are released at the same time Ö (release date of ). The end-to-end deadline of a task is defined by the largest relative deadline of the threads belonging to it. A task is preemptive if all its threads are also preemptive, and thus can be preempted at any time and resumed later.

A task is periodic if the interval between two consecutive releases has a fixed length Ì . Every infinite schedule has a periodic pattern of length Ð Ñ´Ì ½ Ì Ò µ, called the hyperperiod. A task is sporadic if the period between two successive releases is at least Ì units of time. An occurrence of a thread is called a job. The release time Ö (or starting time) of task is the time of its first invocation in the system. A concrete task is a task with a given release time. A set of periodic tasks are synchronous if they are started (i.e. released for the first time) at the same time. If it is not the case, they are said to be asynchronous. Jobs of a periodic task are all released at the same rate Ì . If it is not the case, then sooner or later, one job will miss its deadline. A task is feasible (or schedulable) if all its jobs are completed by their deadlines. Let be the worst-case processing time of a task , then the utilization factor of the processor is È Ì and must be less than or equal to 1 for every feasible task set.

Self-suspension is different from preemption since the status of a suspended task changes (it is not eligible until the external operation is completed). Non-preemptive tasks can self-suspend in order to perform external operations just as preemptive ones do. Furthermore, tasks with selfsuspension extend the classical model of tasks subjected to precedence constraints by assuming suspension delays of length 0 (the external operations is a simple synchronization performed without incurring cost). If a task starts its execution by a self-suspension, then the feasibility problem is equivalent to the release jitter problem. As a consequence, scheduling with self-suspension extends the release jitter problem.

If all delays associated to the self-suspensions of a task are null, then the DAG associated to a task is a precedence graph. In this particular case, it is well-known that an earliest deadline first (EDF) schedule obeys the partial order if the release dates and the deadlines of the threads are consistent with the partial order [20]. But, as we shall see later, such a technique cannot be applied if one of the precedence relations is associated to a non-zero suspension delay.

div.head: Review of known complexity results on one processor
div.p: There are several known complexity results for real-time scheduling. We briefly survey these results for single processor scheduling of independent, periodic and preemptive tasks without self-suspension. The earliest deadline first algorithm (EDF) is known to be optimal [17,15] (i.e. it always finds a feasible schedule if there is one). Let Ò be the number of tasks in the system. Then, verifying that every task, such as Ì , meets its deadline requires Ç´Òµ operations. But as far as we know, the complexity status is open when the condition Ì is removed (pseudopolynomial algorithms are known if ¼ È Ì ½, but we do not know if there exists a fully polynomial time algorithm [4]). If we focus on fixed priority-driven schedules, similar results are known. The deadline monotonic policy is optimal for every synchronous set of tasks if for every task Ì . A polynomial time algorithm exists for verifying that deadlines are met for tasks that satisfy the following conditions:

But, the complexity status of this feasibility problem is unknown if one of these conditions is removed (pseudo-polynomial time algorithms are also available if the utilization factor of the processor is strickly less than 1). The feasibility problem becomes co-AEÈ-hard in the strong sense when asynchronous releases are allowed [4,5]. When the tasks are subjected to asynchronous release times and every task has been assigned a fixed priority, then verifying the feasibility of a fixed-priority schedule is indeed co-AEÈ-hard in the strong sense as well [16].

For sporadic, independent task sets, the related feasibility problem is known to be in co-AEÈ [8]. But, no polynomial time algorithms have been devised yet. However, there exist pseudo-polynomial time algorithms for both preemptive [6] and non-preemptive [13] dispatching strategies, provided that the utilization factor is less than a constant ½. Outline that, most feasibility problems for independent tasks are in co-AEÈ rather than in AEÈ. As a consequence, efficient schedulability tests have been proposed to check that a schedule is unfeasible in a given interval of time [8].

We now focus on sets of dependent, periodic tasks running upon an uniprocessor system. When the tasks share mutual exclusion resources, then verifying feasibility is AEÈ-hard in the strong sense [18]. If all tasks share the same resource, then we deal with a non-preemptive scheduling problem. For recurring real-time tasks (i.e. conditional code is allowed), the related feasibility problem is known to be co-AEÈ-hard for static and dynamic priority-driven scheduling policies [7].

div.head: Non-preemptive sequential tasks
div.p: According to [13], scheduling concrete non-preemptive tasks is AEÈ-hard in the strong sense, but the proof is based on asynchronous tasks. Since non-preemptive tasks are particular cases of non-preemptive tasks with self-suspension, we can conclude that associated feasibility problems are AEÈ-hard in the strong sense as well for asynchronous tasks.

In order to deal with self-suspension of tasks, we can note that preemption is not needed to construct a feasible schedule in the transformations performed in Theorems 1 and 2 (i.e. exactly three tasks start and complete in every idle-time slot). A particular case of threads having equal processing requirements is defined by unit length threads. The next section deals with scheduling multi-threaded tasks having unitlength execution times. But, DAG's of tasks are no longer sets of chains.

div.head: AEÈ-hardness result for multi-threaded tasks
div.p: In the previous section, we considered tasks defined as sequential chains of threads, separated by suspension delays. The processing requirements are positive numbers. We now focus on general multi-threaded tasks.

Without loss of generality, we focus on the feasibility problem for a graph of threads, regardless of the original tasks. We shall prove that the feasibility problem is AEÈhard in the strong sense if every thread has a unit execution time. This assumption is interesting, since numerous scheduling problems are AEÈ-hard when arbitrary processing times are considered, whereas they are polynomial in the case of tasks having unit-length processing times (see for instance Sequencing with release times and deadlines, [10] p. 236). Furthermore, considering threads with unitlength execution times is of theoretical interest since in that way, computational complexity results are simultaneously valid for preemptive and non-preemptive tasks. Such a result has been proved for non-periodic tasks in [9]. These authors have used a very complicated transformation from 3SAT, based on the same initial idea as in the proof performed in [21].

We propose here a simpler proof for periodic tasks. The following reduction uses a multiprocessor scheduling problem, called precedence constrained scheduling [10]. This problem has been shown to be AEÈ-hard in the strong sense in [21].

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Integrating pratical factors in the real-time scheduling theory leads to AEÈ-hardness results, even for single processor problems with independent, synchronous sets of tasks. As a consequence, known results for the feasibility problem while considering priority-driven schedules (EDF, Deadline Monotonic...) are no longer applicable. In this paper, we have studied tasks which can be subjected to selfsuspensions when tasks invoke external operations, such as I/O or remote procedure calls. The kernel temporarily suspends the tasks and then releases them when external operations are completed. Feasibility problems for preemptive and non-preemptive tasks have been proved AEÈ-hard in the strong sense for sequential tasks. When multi-threaded tasks are considered, we have shown that checking feasibility is also AEÈ-hard in the strong sense for unit execution time threads and integer self-suspension delays.
